title: Applying a textured sand finish plaster coat
subtitle: Apply a sand finish plaster coat over a browning or bonding base to give a lightly textured, paint-ready surface
excerpt: How to apply a sand finish plaster top coat over a scratch or browning base. Covers mixing the plaster, applying the first pass in bays to maintain a wet edge, re-passing to close the texture, and floating to the finished profile.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plastering practice and British Gypsum product guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A fine-aggregate top coat plaster containing sand that produces a slightly textured, granular surface when floated rather than the smooth gloss of a multi-finish skim coat. It is applied at 5 to 8 mm thick over a browning or bonding base and finished with a plastic float. Suitable for painting directly without an additional skim.

A lightweight backing plaster used on absorbent masonry surfaces as the undercoat layer before a finish coat. It provides the bulk of the wall thickness and gives a flat, even key for the top coat. Applied in one or two passes to a total thickness of 11 to 14 mm.

The live edge of a plaster coat that has not yet started to set. Working toward and then back from the wet edge allows the new material to blend into the existing coat without a visible join line. Losing the wet edge produces a hard edge between two different set stages that is difficult to finish out.

content.text: A sand finish plaster coat gives a fine, lightly textured surface on a scratch or browning base, suitable for painting directly without skimming. The technique is applied in bays to keep a wet edge and re-passed to close and flatten the texture as the plaster stiffens. INTERMEDIATE: timing and wet-edge management are the key skills.

or bonding base must be set hard and scratch-coated. Dampen it with a brush or spray before applying the finish coat so it does not pull moisture from the fresh plaster too fast. The surface should be damp to the touch but not wet.

Apply the plaster from the hawk with upward strokes of the trowel, covering the wall in a band starting from one side. Maintain the
by working across the wall continuously without stopping. Aim for 5 to 8 mm coat thickness. Cover the full area with the first pass before the material at the starting edge has set.

When the first pass has stiffened enough to resist finger pressure but is still slightly soft, re-pass with the trowel in long, smooth strokes to flatten any ridges and close the surface texture. Follow with the plastic float in circular arcs to even out the texture. Bring water to the surface by misting lightly and trowelling to determine the final texture: more float pressure closes the surface more; less gives a slightly coarser grain.

attrs.symptom: Plaster sets too fast and cannot be re-passed
attrs.cause: The base coat was too dry and drew moisture from the finish coat rapidly, accelerating the set.
attrs.fix: Dampen the base coat more thoroughly before the next application. Work in smaller areas per mix to stay ahead of the set.

attrs.symptom: Hard line visible where one area of plaster meets the next
attrs.cause: The wet edge was lost: the first area started to set before the new area was applied and blended in.
attrs.fix: Work faster and in smaller bays so each new pass overlaps a still-wet edge. Dampen the hard edge and re-work to blend.
